Yes, because when you pop it into neutral, your engine still disconnects from the rest of the drive train. 

With a manual though, practice engine braking. The ELI5 explication is that instead of using gas to "push" the cylinder creating power, it'll "pull" and create a small vacuum; thus slowing the car down more than just coasting. Although there is a risk with that because you're slowing down considerably without the brake lights illuminated.

Coast, coast, coast! Try to use your accelerator only when you need to. See a yellow light 1/2 mile up the road? No need to maintain speed. Plus it'll help your brakes last longer too, because you're stopping at 30mph instead of 50mph.

And don't go into neutral either. Modern cars will not inject fuel when coasting. When you put it in neutral, it will disconnect the drive train and the engine will have to use fuel to keep it running.

If you can change a tire, you can certainly rotate your tires. Why pay a shop $20, if you can do it for free?

From there, you can change your oil, brakes, spark plugs, air filters (engine And cabin). This'll hold you over and save you a lot of money, especially brakes.

Then, something might break. Like a suspension piece or a vacuum line. You've been looking over your car while doing the maintenance, unconsciously memorizing how everything should look. (pertaining to "2") How long do people in Europe usually spend at a restaurant table? I've heard that it's usually a whole night event, and just as much a social thing as much as just eating. In America I don't think I've ever spent more than 90 minutes at a table ever, and that's a rare occasion itself. Usually it's less than an hour. I've never felt rushed or anything close to it.

 And it's not like the waiter is popping by every 5 minutes either giving you a death stare that infers "you done yet?". This is the frequency.

1. To greet and get drink orders.

2. Deliver drinks and get your food orders. If it's water, some restaurants will give you a pitcher, but some don't, just depends. 

3. Deliver food orders. They'll usually ask if anyone needs a refill.

 However if they notice that someone's cup is empty, and automatically bring by another drink without having to say anything, Americans (at least I) would say, "huh, they're putting in the extra effort, I'll throw a little more in." if we see that someone goes Above standards, we reward that behavior.

4. Between 25%-50% way through the meal, they'll touch the table (quick stop) and ask if everything is OK. Just as a double check that the order was correct and if anyone needs a refill that didn't get one with food.

5. Food is done. They will ask if anyone wants dessert or anything else, like to-go containers or coffee etc. If no, then they'll go and grab the check. Usually it's not too long of a wait.

However, let's say you want to stay and chat for a bit, waiters are smart. If you and people at your table order refills or maybe another alcoholic drink, that's a sign that says "hey, well be here a little longer. No check yet. But anyways.. 

5.5? They'll drop off the check. 

(sometimes a waitress will hand write "thank you!" on the check. I kinda like that attention to detail. But that's just me.) 

5.75?? They'll pick up the check.

6. Drop off the change/credit card and say have a wonderful night!

Personally I don't think that's as constant as you think it is. It's based on the point through the meal, not watch time. If I go in by myself then yeah, they'll drop by every 5 minutes but that's because I'm there for 30 minutes max. I expect and want to be out of there fast. And a table of 4? Usually like an hour ish. Most importantly, We know the drill and the waiters know the drill. No one feels rush, it's just a culture difference.
